solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Typical Englishman can intimidate last to go

parts.note: can is slang for a lavatory, as is john

indicators.note: the final letter of the synonym for intimidate is dropped, so its last letter goes

parts.note: to intimidate someone is to bully them

explanation.surface: An Englishman of the stereotypical sort is apparently fond of browbeating people until the last one leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last to go' removes the Y from BULLY, leaving BULL. 'can' is American slang for a toilet, the same as JOHN.
explanation.definitionFit: The national personification of England, a stout farmer in a Union Jack waistcoat, stands for the typical Englishman.

clue.text: Militants in Jordan's capital owned 11 boxes

definitions.note: plural in the clue; the answer is used as a collective or plural noun for holy warriors

indicators.note: a capital letter here means the first letter of the word Jordan
boxes means the two ones enclose the synonym for owned

parts.note: the number 11 written as two Roman ones side by side
owned means had

explanation.surface: Fighters in the Jordanian capital keep eleven crates of weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like a cross-reference to 11-down, but here it is simply two ones, II, which 'boxes' wraps round HAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighters waging a holy war in the name of Islam are militants of a radical kind.

clue.text: Pay for it to cure anorexic? Sure can, if ordered

parts.note: to cure is to heal
someone anorexic is very thin

indicators.note: ordered means the letters of sure can are put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you can pay to treat an eating disorder and gets a cheerful yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if ordered' rearranges SURECAN to INSURANCE, completing the phrase after HEAL and THIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A policy for medical cover pays the bills for treatment, so you pay for it in premiums.

clue.text: 7 contains total nonsense

indicators.note: contains means the abbreviation holds the synonym for total inside it

parts.note: 7-down is a building society, abbreviated BS
total means all

explanation.surface: A building society holds utter rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' refers to 7-down, BUILDING SOCIETY, whose usual abbreviation is BS; 'contains' puts ALL inside it. 'Total nonsense' looks like one phrase but splits into total (ALL) and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for rubbish, as in an exclamation of disbelief at something untrue.

clue.text: Gaps ruined a clue about an uprising

indicators.note: about means the scrambled letters go round the other piece
ruined means the letters of a clue are wrecked and rebuilt
in a down clue an uprising means the word an is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Somebody has spoilt a crossword clue about a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' turns A CLUE into LACUE; 'uprising' turns AN into NA, and 'about' puts LACUE round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Missing portions in a text or a manuscript are lacunae, the Latin plural for holes or blanks.

clue.text: Firm's small board

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a board is a table, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A company's modest board of directors.
explanation.definitionFit: Something firm is steady and secure, not wobbly.

clue.text: She's willing to try adult jokes on radio

parts.note: to try is to test
A is the film certificate abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: on radio means the word is heard rather than seen, so tricks gives a same-sounding spelling

parts.note: jokes are tricks, as in practical jokes

explanation.surface: A woman who is game to try out risqué humour on the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She's willing' reads as eager, but it means she is making a will. 'on radio' turns TRICKS into TRIX by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A female maker of a will, the feminine of testator, is literally a woman who is making her will.

clue.text: City in US obliged nervous buyers to borrow from it

indicators.note: nervous suggests the letters are jittery and fall into a new order

explanation.surface: An American city made anxious homebuyers take out loans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nervous' rearranges CITY IN US OBLIGED; the place names are misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A British mutual lender that offers mortgages to people purchasing homes.

clue.text: Writer's French art, for example, is in Berlin

parts.note: in archaic English art is thou art; the French for you are, tu es, gives es
say means for example
the German word for is is ist

explanation.surface: A French artwork, for instance, is on display in the German capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is the old verb (thou art), whose French form is ES (tu es); 'is in Berlin' is German IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who composes short prose pieces on a subject is a kind of writer.

clue.text: Sick child catches each European infestation

indicators.note: catches means the jumbled letters take in the abbreviation for each
sick means the letters of child are unwell and jumbled

parts.note: EA is the abbreviation for each, as on price lists

explanation.surface: An ill youngster has picked up a parasite outbreak, as every European family dreads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick' rearranges CHILD to HDLIC; 'catches' puts EA inside it after the H, and E follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An outbreak of parasitic insects in the hair, common among schoolchildren, is a classic infestation.

clue.text: Quartermaster's hard drinks passed round decoys

parts.note: Q, the gadget man in the Bond films, is the quartermaster

indicators.note: passed round means the synonym for drinks goes round the abbreviation for hard

parts.note: to drink a little is to sip, so drinks gives sips
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: An army supply officer's strong liquor is handed round to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passed round' puts SIPS round H. Q-ships were armed merchant vessels in the World Wars, disguised to lure submarines.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed vessels disguised as harmless merchant ships served to lure enemy submarines into range.

clue.text: Battery cells

parts.note: reads as power units in a battery, but means the reproductive cells laid by battery hens

explanation.definitionFit: Hens kept in battery cages lay these, and each one is a single cell.

clue.text: Takes out fruit

explanation.surface: Someone removes fruit from a bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone out romantically is to go on outings with them; the fruit of a palm is another sense.

clue.text: Tight-fisted tailor lying about pullover?

indicators.note: about means the reworked letters go round the piece from pullover
to tailor is to cut and alter, so the letters of lying are reshaped

parts.note: read as pull over: pull is drag, and over turns it backwards

explanation.surface: A stingy dressmaker fibs about the price of a jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pullover' splits into pull (DRAG) and over, which reads it backwards as GARD; 'tailor' turns LYING into NIGLY, and 'about' puts it round GARD. A pullover is a British jumper, a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mean with money, grudging every penny, is tight-fisted.

clue.text: The sort of interest politician stupidly lies about?

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the abbreviation for politician
stupidly means the letters of lies are thrown about foolishly

parts.note: MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: Asks what kind of interest a politician might fib about through foolishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupidly' turns LIES into SILE; 'about' puts it round MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest calculated only on the original principal, not on accumulated interest, is one kind of interest.

clue.text: Ship in, say, accident traps conscript

indicators.note: traps means the word for an accident encloses the rest

parts.note: a prang is British slang for a minor crash

indicators.note: in means the steamship abbreviation sits inside the abbreviation for say

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A vessel comes to grief in a crash and someone is forced into service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts SS inside EG to make ESSG, and 'traps' puts PRANG round that. PRANG is British slang for a car accident.
explanation.definitionFit: To force someone into service against their will, as naval gangs once seized men for ships.

clue.text: Trick cyclists' contracts

explanation.surface: Agreements signed by stunt riders on bikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Trick cyclist is British rhyming slang for psychiatrist, and head doctors are also called this; it also means gets smaller.

clue.text: Everybody's hoping franchise is secured

indicators.note: secured means the answer is held inside the words everybody's hoping

explanation.surface: All are wishing that a business licence is obtained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secured' points to the run hidden across 'everyBODY'S HOPing'. The Body Shop is a British cosmetics chain run as franchises.
explanation.definitionFit: A British cosmetics retailer with many shops run under licence as franchised outlets.

clue.text: Shy people unknown in refurbished stores

indicators.note: in means the unknown goes inside the rearranged letters
refurbished means the letters of stores are done up into a new order

parts.note: Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Retiring types turn up in shops that have been done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refurbished' turns STORES into OSTERS, and 'in' puts Y inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellfish that clam up tight are proverbially uncommunicative, so reticent folk are likened to them.

clue.text: Fraud in posh part of London's variable

parts.note: SW1 is the postcode of Westminster and Belgravia, with the 1 read as I
Z is an algebraic variable

explanation.surface: A swindle in a smart London district is liable to change.
explanation.walkthrough: SW1 is the postcode for an expensive area of central London; its 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal word for a swindle or a disappointing con.

clue.text: Chauvinistic teams split group

indicators.note: split means the word for group is broken open to take the other piece

parts.note: a group is a set
XI is eleven, a cricket or football team, so teams is XIS

explanation.surface: Bigoted sides break up a group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split' opens SET to take XIS. A side of eleven players is written XI, the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing prejudice against women, as a male chauvinist does.

clue.text: Ghost could give you the creeps if he came in

indicators.note: could give you signals that the letters of the creeps can be rebuilt from the answer with another word added

parts.note: he is the word that came in, added to the answer's letters

explanation.surface: A ghost would frighten you if he entered the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could give you' with 'if he came in' says that the answer's letters plus HE, rearranged, would make THE CREEPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom or apparition is a spirit of the dead.

clue.text: After long periods 3's completely removed

parts.note: long periods of history are eras
3-down is BALLS, and Ed Balls is a British politician, so its first name is Ed

explanation.surface: A recording is wiped clean after many ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets ED after ERAS. Ed Balls is a former Labour cabinet minister, now a TV presenter, so 3's first name gives ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiped out entirely so no trace is left.

clue.text: Two kings in elaborate hosiery riding here

indicators.note: in means the two king abbreviations sit inside the rearranged letters
elaborate means the letters of hosiery are worked into a fancy new order

parts.note: R (Rex) and K are two abbreviations for king

explanation.surface: Two monarchs ride horses wearing fancy stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elaborate' turns HOSIERY into YOSHIRE, and 'in' puts RK inside it. The Ridings were the three historic divisions of this English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic county was divided into three ridings, North, East and West, so a riding is found there.

clue.text: Rector's assistant about to follow sixth rector

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral for six, so sixth
CA (circa) means about

explanation.surface: An assistant to a parish priest is set to succeed the sixth holder of the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' sets CA after VI, with R ending the run.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Church of England a curate or deputy priest who assists a rector; a parish priest serving under one.

clue.text: Is it venomous if prodded initially with ruler?

definitions.text: Is it venomous if prodded initially with ruler?

indicators.note: initially means the first letters of the words venomous, if, prodded are taken

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is a ruler

explanation.surface: Asks whether a snake turns nasty when poked with a measuring stick.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruler is the Queen, ER, not a measuring stick. The whole clue also describes the snake.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder of Britain and its relatives are poisonous snakes that bite when provoked.

clue.text: Airport building's no good in fog

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation sits inside the word for fog

parts.note: a haar is a cold sea fog on the east coast of Britain

explanation.surface: An airport shed is useless in mist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts NG inside HAAR, a Scottish and north-east English word for sea mist.
explanation.definitionFit: A large shed where aircraft are housed and serviced.

clue.text: Misusing these in office may result in plasters

definitions.text: Misusing these in office may result in plasters

indicators.note: misusing means the letters are mishandled and fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Careless use of office equipment ends in sticking plasters on fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram runs the other way: 'Misusing' the answer's letters gives PLASTERS, so PLASTERS rearranged gives the answer. Plasters are British sticking bandages.
explanation.definitionFit: Desk devices that drive wire clips through paper can easily pierce a careless finger.

clue.text: Place on border gives undertaking

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names
a border is an edge

explanation.surface: Siting something at the boundary amounts to a commitment.
explanation.definitionFit: A solemn promise or commitment to do something.

clue.text: Paid rural department with regular yield

parts.note: DEFRA is the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

indicators.note: regular means every other letter of yield is taken

explanation.surface: The countryside ministry paid out with a steady harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular' takes Y, E and D from YIELD. DEFRA is the British government department for farming and the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet costs or expenses is to settle them, so paid them off.
